title: Jonah

stories.title: 🌊 Jonah 1
summaryBullets: Now the word of the LORD came to Jonah son of Amittai, saying, (1:1).
“Get up! Go to the great city of Nineveh and preach against it, because its wickedness has come up before Me.” (1:2).

Jonah, however, got up to flee to Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD. He went down to Joppa and found a ship bound for Tarshish. So he paid the fare and went aboard to sail for Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD. (1:3).
Then the LORD hurled a great wind upon the sea, and such a violent storm arose that the ship was in danger of breaking apart. (1:4).

The sailors were afraid, and each cried out to his own god. And they threw the ship’s cargo into the sea to lighten the load. But Jonah had gone down to the lowest part of the vessel, where he lay down and fell into a deep sleep. (1:5).
The captain approached him and said, “How can you sleep? Get up and call upon your God. Perhaps this God will consider us, so that we may not perish.” (1:6).
“Come!” said the sailors to one another. “Let us cast lots to find out who is responsible for this calamity that is upon us.” So they cast lots, and the lot fell on Jonah. (1:7).
“Tell us now,” they demanded, “who is to blame for this calamity that is upon us? What is your occupation, and where have you come from? What is your country, and who are your people?” (1:8).
“I am a Hebrew,” replied Jonah. “I worship the LORD, the God of the heavens, who made the sea and the dry land.” (1:9).
Then the men were even more afraid and said to him, “What have you done?” The men knew that he was fleeing from the presence of the LORD, because he had told them. (1:10).
Now the sea was growing worse and worse, so they said to Jonah, “What must we do to you to calm this sea for us?” (1:11).
“Pick me up,” he answered, “and cast me into the sea, so it may quiet down for you. For I know that I am to blame for this violent storm that has come upon you.” (1:12).
Nevertheless, the men rowed hard to get back to dry land, but they could not, for the sea was raging against them more and more. (1:13).
So they cried out to the LORD: “Please, O LORD, do not let us perish on account of this man’s life! Do not charge us with innocent blood! For You, O LORD, have done as You pleased.” (1:14).
Then they picked up Jonah and cast him into the sea, and the raging sea grew calm. (1:15).
Then the men feared the LORD greatly, and they offered a sacrifice to the LORD and made vows to Him. (1:16).
Now the LORD had appointed a great fish to swallow Jonah, and Jonah spent three days and three nights in the belly of the fish. (1:17).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 14:25: Jonah son of Amittai mentioned in the reign of Jeroboam II.
Psalm 107:23–30: Sailors in a storm cry out and are delivered.
Matthew 12:40: “Sign of Jonah” (three days and three nights).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תַּרְשִׁישׁ (Tarshish), Greek (LXX): Θαρσείς, Aramaic: תרשיש
translationNotes.note: Distant seaport; exact location debated in antiquity. Emphasizes Jonah’s attempt to go far from his assignment.

translationNotes.term: From the presence of the LORD
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִלִּפְנֵי יְהוָה (milifnê YHWH), Greek (LXX): ἀπὸ προσώπου Κυρίου, Aramaic: מן קדם יי
translationNotes.note: Means fleeing the LORD’s commission/face, not denying God’s omnipresence.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הִפִּילוּ גּוֹרָלוֹת (hippîlū gōrālōt), Greek (LXX): ἔβαλον κλήρους, Aramaic: פלו פוריא
translationNotes.note: Ancient method to identify responsibility or make decisions (1:7).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דָּג גָּדוֹל (dag gadol), Greek (LXX): κῆτος (kētos, ‘sea creature’), Aramaic: נונא רבא
translationNotes.note: Not specified as a whale; a large sea creature appointed by God (1:17).

stories.keyTakeaway: Jonah flees his mission; God sends a storm; the sailors end up worshiping the LORD; a great fish swallows Jonah for three days and nights.

stories.title: 🐟 Jonah 2
summaryBullets: From inside the fish, Jonah prayed to the LORD his God, (2:1).
saying: “In my distress I called to the LORD, and He answered me. From the belly of Sheol I called for help, and You heard my voice. (2:2).
For You cast me into the deep, into the heart of the seas, and the current swirled about me; all Your breakers and waves swept over me. (2:3).
At this, I said, ‘I have been banished from Your sight; yet I will look once more toward Your holy temple.’ (2:4).
The waters engulfed me to take my life; the watery depths closed around me; the seaweed wrapped around my head. (2:5).
To the roots of the mountains I descended; the earth beneath me barred me in forever! But You raised my life from the pit, O LORD my God! (2:6).
As my life was fading away, I remembered the LORD. My prayer went up to You, to Your holy temple. (2:7).
Those who cling to worthless idols forsake His loving devotion. (2:8).
But I, with the voice of thanksgiving, will sacrifice to You. I will fulfill what I have vowed. Salvation is from the LORD!” (2:9).
And the LORD commanded the fish, and it vomited Jonah onto dry land. (2:10).
crossRefs: Psalm 18:4–6: Cords of Sheol and distress in deep waters.
Psalm 42:7: “All your waves and breakers have gone over me.”
Luke 11:30: Jonah as a sign to a city.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁאוֹל (Sheol), בּוֹר (bor, ‘pit’), Greek (LXX): ᾅδης, λάκκος, Aramaic: שאולא, בורא
translationNotes.note: Realm of the dead / place of descent in Jonah’s prayer (2:2-6).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֶסֶד (ḥesed), Greek (LXX): ἔλεος, Aramaic: חסדא
translationNotes.note: Covenant loyalty Jonah says idol-clingers abandon (2:8).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וַיְצַו (waytsav), Greek (LXX): ἐνετείλατο, Aramaic: פקד
translationNotes.note: God’s direct control over the creature (2:10).

The Old Testament realm of the dead; a shadowy underworld where both righteous and wicked descend (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not necessarily a place of torment; more a state of cessation and silence. The Septuagint and New Testament render it with the Greek word hades.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jonah prays from the depths and is delivered; the fish releases him onto land by God’s command.

stories.title: 🏙️ Jonah 3
summaryBullets: Then the word of the LORD came to Jonah a second time: (3:1).
“Get up! Go to the great city of Nineveh and proclaim to it the message that I give you.” (3:2).
This time Jonah got up and went to Nineveh, in accordance with the word of the LORD. Now Nineveh was an exceedingly great city, requiring a three-day journey. (3:3).
On the first day of his journey, Jonah set out into the city and proclaimed, “Forty more days and Nineveh will be overturned!” (3:4).
And the Ninevites believed God. They proclaimed a fast and dressed in sackcloth, from the greatest of them to the least. (3:5).
When word reached the king of Nineveh, he got up from his throne, took off his royal robe, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes. (3:6).
Then he issued a proclamation in Nineveh: “By the decree of the king and his nobles: Let no man or beast, herd or flock, taste anything at all. They must not eat or drink. (3:7).
Furthermore, let both man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and have everyone call out earnestly to God. Let each one turn from his evil ways and from the violence in his hands. (3:8).
Who knows? God may turn and relent; He may turn from His fierce anger, so that we will not perish.” (3:9).
When God saw their actions— that they had turned from their evil ways— He relented from the disaster He had threatened to bring upon them. (3:10).
crossRefs: Jeremiah 18:7–8: God relents concerning disaster when a nation turns from evil.
Matthew 12:41: People of Nineveh will rise in judgment (later statement).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נֶהְפָּכֶת (nehpākhet, from הָפַךְ haphakh), Greek (LXX): καταστραφήσεται, Aramaic: תתהפך
translationNotes.note: Can mean overturned/destroyed; the verb has a range including ‘turn/transform,’ but here announces coming ruin in forty days (3:4).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נִחָם (niḥam, ‘be moved to pity/relent’), Greek (LXX): μετενόησεν, Aramaic: אתנחם
translationNotes.note: Human-facing language for God holding back announced disaster when people turn from evil (3:10).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חָמָס (ḥāmās), Greek (LXX): ἀδικία/βία, Aramaic: חמסא
translationNotes.note: Named explicitly in the king’s decree as sin that must stop (3:8).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַהֲלַךְ שְׁלֹשֶׁת יָמִים (mahalakh sheloshet yamim), Greek (LXX): πορεία τριῶν ἡμερῶν, Aramaic: הילוך תלתא יומין
translationNotes.note: Idiomatic measure of civic size/route; indicates a very large urban area (3:3).

A coarse, dark goat-hair fabric worn against bare skin as a universal sign of mourning, repentance, or distress (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5; Matthew 11:21). Wearing it publicly broadcast grief or contrition; the discomfort itself was part of the symbolism.

stories.keyTakeaway: God gives Jonah a second chance; Nineveh responds with citywide fasting and turning from evil; God relents from the announced disaster.

stories.title: 🌞 Jonah 4
summaryBullets: Jonah, however, was greatly displeased, and he became angry. (4:1).

So he prayed to the LORD, saying, “O LORD, is this not what I said while I was still in my own country? This is why I was so quick to flee toward Tarshish. I knew that You are a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion — One who relents from sending disaster. (4:2).
And now, O LORD, please take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live.” (4:3).
But the LORD replied, “Have you any right to be angry?” (4:4).
Then Jonah left the city and sat down east of it, where he made himself a shelter and sat in its shade to see what would happen to the city. (4:5).
So the LORD God appointed a vine, and it grew up to provide shade over Jonah’s head to ease his discomfort, and Jonah was greatly pleased with the plant. (4:6).
When dawn came the next day, God appointed a worm that attacked the plant so that it withered. (4:7).
As the sun was rising, God appointed a scorching east wind, and the sun beat down on Jonah’s head so that he grew faint and wished to die, saying, “It is better for me to die than to live.” (4:8).
Then God asked Jonah, “Have you any right to be angry about the plant?” “I do,” he replied. “I am angry enough to die!” (4:9).
But the LORD said, “You cared about the plant, which you neither tended nor made grow. It sprang up in a night and perished in a night. (4:10).
So should I not care about the great city of Nineveh, which has more than 120,000 people who cannot tell their right hand from their left, and many cattle as well?” (4:11).
crossRefs: Exodus 34:6–7: God’s character formula (gracious and compassionate).
Joel 2:13: Similar description of the LORD’s mercy.
Psalm 145:8–9: The LORD is gracious, compassionate, and good to all.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָנָה (manāh, ‘appoint/assign’), Greek (LXX): κατέστησεν/διέταξεν, Aramaic: מנא
translationNotes.note: Used repeatedly: God appoints the fish, plant, worm, and east wind (1:17) (4:6–8).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קִיקָיוֹן (qiqāyōn), Greek (LXX): κολοκύνθη (var.), Aramaic: קיקיון
translationNotes.note: Exact species uncertain (suggestions include castor-oil plant).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קָדִים (qadīm), Greek (LXX): καύσων/νότος (var.), Aramaic: קדים
translationNotes.note: Hot, desiccating wind known for causing severe heat (4:8).

translationNotes.term: Do not know right hand from left
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֹא יָדְעוּ בֵּין יְמִין לִשְׂמֹאול (lo yādaʿū bein yemin lismoʾl), Greek (LXX): οὐκ ἴσασι δεξιὰν ἀπὸ ἀριστερᾶς, Aramaic: לא ידעין בין ימינא לשמאלא
translationNotes.note: Expression for moral/spiritual ignorance, including many children; the verse also notes many animals (4:11).

stories.keyTakeaway: God confronts Jonah’s anger with a plant, a worm, and a hot wind, ending with a question that contrasts Jonah’s short-lived pity with God’s care for a great city.

headings.text: Jonah’s Anger at the Lord’s Compassion

intro:
Jonah was written by Jonah son of Amittai (Jonah 1:1), the prophet from the northern kingdom of Israel during the reign of Jeroboam II (793-753 BC). 2 Kings 14:25 identifies him as "Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet from Gath-Hepher," who had earlier prophesied that Jeroboam II would restore Israel's territorial boundaries "from the entrance of Hamath to the Sea of the Arabah," a prophecy that was fulfilled during Jeroboam's reign. The book bearing his name was composed during the same general period, around the mid-eighth century BC (c. 770-750 BC). Jonah was a Galilean, native of Gath-Hepher in the territory of Zebulun (Joshua 19:13), a small village about three miles north of Nazareth (the modern site of Khirbet az-Zurra near el-Mashhad preserves what tradition has identified as Jonah's tomb). He was a contemporary of Amos (the Judahite shepherd who ministered in the north) and the slightly younger Hosea (the northern-native prophet), all three working in the same generation as Israel's prosperity reached its peak. The prophet's name Yonah (יוֹנָה) means "dove." Jonah ben Amittai is the only prophet of this name in the Old Testament; he is distinct from Jonah/John the father of Simon Peter (referenced in Matthew 16:17 "Simon bar-Jonah" and John 1:42; 21:15-17, an unrelated first-century figure).

The historical setting is the era when the Neo-Assyrian Empire was temporarily weakened, between the strong reign of Adad-nirari III (810-783 BC) and the rise of Tiglath-Pileser III (745-727 BC). Three weak kings ruled Assyria during this window: Shalmaneser IV (783-773 BC), Ashur-dan III (773-755 BC), and Ashur-nirari V (755-745 BC). Jonah's mission to Nineveh probably took place during Ashur-dan III's reign, an unsettled period in Assyrian history. The Assyrian eponym lists record a total solar eclipse on June 15, 763 BC (visible from Nineveh and central Assyria), plus famines, plagues, and a revolt in the city of Ashur in 763-758 BC; the combination may help explain why a city of Assyria's brutality would be receptive to a foreign prophet's warning of impending judgment. Nineveh sat on the east bank of the Tigris River opposite modern Mosul in northern Iraq; the city was massive in Jonah's day, with surrounding satellite cities forming what the book describes as "an exceedingly great city, a three-days' journey across" (Jonah 3:3, likely referring to the entire metropolitan area of the Nineveh plain). The city's recorded repentance under Jonah's preaching delayed its destruction by more than a century; Nineveh ultimately fell to a Babylonian-Median coalition in 612 BC (the event prophesied in Nahum a generation before its fulfillment).

Jonah is the thirty-second book of the Christian Old Testament and the fifth of the twelve Minor Prophets. The Hebrew name Yonah (יוֹנָה) is the prophet's own name. Jonah is unique among the Minor Prophets: rather than a collection of oracles delivered by the prophet, the book is a narrative about the prophet himself, with only one short oracle quoted (Jonah 3:4, the five-word warning to Nineveh in Hebrew: "Forty more days, and Nineveh will be overthrown"). Hebrew manuscript fragments of Jonah were among the Dead Sea Scrolls discovered at Qumran (mid-20th century AD), preserved as part of the Twelve Minor Prophets scrolls; the earliest copies date to the 2nd century BC. Jesus referenced Jonah's experience in the great fish as a sign of His own death and resurrection (Matthew 12:38-41; 16:1-4; Luke 11:29-32), declaring that "as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth" (Matthew 12:40), and that the men of Nineveh would rise up at judgment to condemn His generation because they had repented at Jonah's preaching while His generation had refused to repent at the preaching of "one greater than Jonah" (Matthew 12:41).
